walkthroughs.body_html:
Programming Languages & IDEs — a core area of GCSE Computer Science.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Programming Languages & IDEs brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Programming Languages & IDEs.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which translator produces a standalone executable file?
options: A compiler
An interpreter
A trace table
A linker-free editor

mcqs.q: One advantage of high-level languages over low-level languages is that they are:
options: Closer to natural language, so quicker to write and easier to debug
Executed directly by the CPU with no translation
Impossible to make errors in
Only usable on one specific processor

mcqs.q: Which IDE feature lets you pause a running program at a chosen line to inspect variable values?
options: A breakpoint in the debugger
The spell checker
The colour theme picker
The zoom control

mcqs.q: Does an interpreter create a machine-code file you can run later?
options: Yes - interpreters and compilers both output an executable file.
Yes - assembly is a high-level language like Python.
No - an interpreter translates and executes the program line by line each run and saves no executable; producing a stored executable is what compilers do.
Yes - interpreters save their translation as a text document.

mcqs.q: Are assembly language and machine code the same thing?
options: No - assembly uses human-readable mnemonics like ADD and LDA that map one-to-one onto machine code's binary instructions; an assembler converts between them.
Yes - assembly is just machine code printed on paper.
Yes - installing an IDE installs a new language automatically.
Yes - assembly is a high-level language like Python.

mcqs.q: Is an IDE a programming language?
options: Yes - installing an IDE installs a new language automatically.
No - an IDE is a software tool for writing, running and debugging programs; the language is what you write, the IDE is where you write it.
Yes - interpreters save their translation as a text document.
Yes - Python and an IDE are the same kind of thing.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “High-level language”?
options: The binary instructions a CPU executes directly; every program must ultimately become machine code to run.
A programming language, such as Python, with English-like keywords that is easy for humans to read, write and debug, and portable between machines.
A translator that converts an entire high-level program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file and a list of all errors.
A translator that reads, translates and executes a high-level program line by line each time it runs, stopping when it meets an error.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Interpreter”?
options: A programming language, such as Python, with English-like keywords that is easy for humans to read, write and debug, and portable between machines.
Assembly language and machine code, which closely match the processor's own instruction set and give fine control over the hardware.
A translator that reads, translates and executes a high-level program line by line each time it runs, stopping when it meets an error.
An integrated development environment bundling an editor, error diagnostics, a run-time environment and debugging tools to help programmers write code.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Machine code”?
options: The binary instructions a CPU executes directly; every program must ultimately become machine code to run.
A translator that reads, translates and executes a high-level program line by line each time it runs, stopping when it meets an error.
A translator that converts an entire high-level program into machine code in one go, producing an executable file and a list of all errors.
Assembly language and machine code, which closely match the processor's own instruction set and give fine control over the hardware.
